content: In regions with low prevalence of onchocerciasis due to mass drug administration (MDA), the applicability of diagnostic studies for detecting onchocerciasis in humans was unclear in seven out of eleven studies, low in two studies, and high in two others. Concerns about applicability were primarily due to the fact that the populations studied often had high microfilarial prevalence, which does not reflect populations with low prevalence resulting from MDA. Two distinct bodies of evidence were used to assess the quality of evidence for each comparison: observational evidence and diagnostic study evidence. Based on two prospective observational studies, skin snip microscopy, Ov-16 serology, ocular morbidity assessments, and O-150 PCR (Poolscreen) in black flies reliably demonstrated the interruption of Onchocerca volvulus transmission after MDA initiation and the elimination of onchocerciasis after MDA cessation. The quality of evidence was low for most methods except for O-150 PCR in black flies, which had high-quality evidence. Seven diagnostic studies showed that O-150 PCR of skin snips had diagnostic test accuracy (DTA) values at least as accurate as skin snip microscopy, with potentially better sensitivity in low-prevalence settings due to MDA. Four diagnostic studies indicated that Ov-16 serology had DTA values comparable to skin snip microscopy, with potentially better sensitivity in low-prevalence settings, while performance was similar in high-prevalence settings. Four studies demonstrated that O-150 PCR (Poolscreen) in black flies was as effective as black fly dissection in detecting infective Onchocerca volvulus larvae. Although initial costs for O-150 PCR were higher than dissection, subsequent costs were lower, and newer DNA extraction methods with larger pool sizes could further reduce costs. No evidence was found regarding the optimal timing or cut-off points for testing. One observational study suggested that the best time to demonstrate the interruption of transmission after MDA initiation varied between different foci. Limitations in study design, such as reliance on skin snip microscopy as the reference test, prevent conclusions about whether comparator index tests have superior DTA characteristics. For example, O-150 PCR of skin snips and Ov-16 serology were shown to be at least as good as skin snip microscopy, but the reliability of skin snip microscopy as a gold-standard reference test is questionable, especially in low-prevalence settings. The included studies were conducted in Africa and the Americas, such as Uganda and Ecuador. Two prospective observational studies provided data on the clinical pathway, while 15 diagnostic studies provided information on specific parts of the evidence chain. Many studies operationalized the 2001 WHO criteria for verifying onchocerciasis elimination but lacked longitudinal data or comparisons, limiting their inclusion in formal evidence synthesis. Epidemiological evaluations in observational studies used skin snip microscopy, Ov-16 serology, slit lamp examinations, and O-150 PCR (Poolscreen) in black flies. Skin snip microscopy and O-150 PCR reliably demonstrated the interruption of transmission after 12–16 years of MDA and the elimination of onchocerciasis 2–5 years after MDA cessation. However, the quality of evidence was low for skin snip microscopy, ocular morbidity, and Ov-16 serology due to indirectness, bias, or imprecision, while it was high for O-150 PCR in black flies. The main weaknesses of these studies included the lack of comparison groups and inconsistencies in the number of villages and individuals studied at different time points. Results from African foci may not be generalizable to other regions, and Ov-16 serology results from the Americas may not apply to other continents. Additionally, Ov-16 serology and ocular morbidity assessments were verified during post-treatment surveillance using O-150 PCR in black flies and other serological surveys, leading to a downgrade in evidence quality due to bias. Although WHO reports certification of elimination in several countries, no comparative testing data or follow-up reports were found to assess the reliability of testing regimes. Apart from the two included observational studies, no other publicly available reports presented post-treatment surveillance data to confirm the interruption of Onchocerca volvulus transmission. In summary, while O-150 PCR (Poolscreen) in black flies demonstrated high-quality evidence for detecting transmission interruption and elimination, other diagnostic methods like skin snip microscopy and Ov-16 serology had lower-quality evidence due to limitations in study design and indirectness. Further research is needed to establish reliable testing protocols and validate diagnostic methods across diverse settings.
